questions.explanation: Bosede Ademilua-Afolayan is the author of the play, which is listed on the WAEC Literature-in-English syllabus for 2026-2030 .

questions.text: What is the full birth name of the character who becomes King Ajanaku?
options: Olaniyonu
Odejimi
Ogundele
Odekunle
questions.explanation: Olaniyonu is the birth name of Ajanaku, the illegitimate son of Serubawon and Adebisi who is falsely presented as King Akinjobi's son .

questions.text: What does the name 'Ajanaku' mean in Yoruba?
options: Lion
Elephant
Tiger
Buffalo
questions.explanation: Ajanaku is the Yoruba word for elephant, symbolizing immense power and the arrogance that comes with it .

questions.text: What is the name of the ritual that Ajanaku undergoes in his quest for immortality?
options: Olubori
Ijedodo
Egungun
Ifa
questions.explanation: The Ijedodo ritual requires the blood of virgins to sustain the king's life and grant him immortality .

questions.text: What does the Ijedodo ritual require as a sacrifice?
options: goat
The blood of virgins
white ram
Gold and silver
questions.explanation: The Ijedodo charm feeds on the blood of virgins, who are raped and die slow, painful deaths .

questions.text: Who is Desola, and why is she significant in the play?
options: She is the queen.
She is Serubawon's daughter and the sixth virgin victim of the Ijedodo ritual.
She is Iya Agba's granddaughter.
She is a market trader.
questions.explanation: Desola is Serubawon's only daughter. Her selection as the final virgin for the Ijedodo ritual represents tragic irony and poetic justice .

questions.text: What happens to Serubawon at the end of the play?
options: He becomes the new king.
He is pardoned by the community.
He commits suicide after being exposed.
He flees to another village.
questions.explanation: Serubawon commits suicide after his role in the corruption and tyranny is exposed, representing the playwright's verdict on those who trade integrity for power .

questions.text: What is the primary source of the play's stylistic inspiration?
options: Western theatre traditions.
Yoruba oral traditions, including proverbs, folktales, and rituals.
Greek tragedy.
Shakespearean drama.
questions.explanation: Ademilua-Afolayan draws heavily on Yoruba orature, including proverbs, folktales, and cultural practices, to craft an authentic African drama .

questions.text: Who says: 'I don't call him Uncle because that's the title you all recognise him with; I call him Uncle because he is truly my uncle'?
options: Taye to Mama
Bolaji to Femi
Odekunle to Desola
Ogundele to Odejimi
questions.explanation: This quotation is from 'The Drama of Taye & Bolaji', not from 'Once Upon an Elephant'. The correct answer for 'Once Upon an Elephant' quotations would be different.

questions.text: Who says: 'You were supposed to win this contest, but she has diverted your destiny and given it to her son'?
options: Aunty Sewa to Uncle Makinde
Madam Bisola to Korede
Mama Titi to Taye
Femi to Bolaji
questions.explanation: This quotation is from 'The Drama of Taye & Bolaji', not from 'Once Upon an Elephant'. The correct answer for 'Once Upon an Elephant' quotations would be different.

questions.text: What is the contextual significance of Iya Agba's statement that Ajanaku is 'a black pigeon in a poultry of well-bred fowls'?
options: It praises Ajanaku's uniqueness.
It implies that Ajanaku is an outsider and impostor who does not belong among the royal lineage.
It describes the palace poultry.
It has no significant meaning.
questions.explanation: Iya Agba's metaphor implies that Ajanaku is an outsider and impostor who does not belong among the royal lineage, reinforcing her claim about his illegitimacy .

questions.text: Who says: 'God, why do the wicked always succeed? Why do the good people end up being enslaved by reckless sinners?'
options: Iya Agba
Ajanaku
This quotation is not from 'Once Upon an Elephant'
Odejimi
questions.explanation: This quotation is from 'The Drama of Taye & Bolaji', not from 'Once Upon an Elephant'.

questions.text: How does the play's pre-colonial Yoruba setting function as a vehicle for contemporary political critique, and what does this reveal about the relationship between historical fiction and political commentary?
options: It is purely a historical recreation with no contemporary relevance.

It allows the playwright to use Yoruba oral traditions to allegorically critique contemporary Nigerian and African politics, demonstrating how historical fiction can serve as a vehicle for political commentary.
It celebrates the superiority of pre-colonial governance over modern democracy.
It has no particular significance for understanding the play's politics.
questions.explanation: The pre-colonial setting allows the playwright to draw on Yoruba oral traditions to create a culturally grounded allegory about tyranny and resistance that speaks to contemporary African realities .

questions.text: How does the play engage with the Yoruba concept of 'àló' (folktale) as a structuring device for political critique?
options: It rejects folktales as outdated and irrelevant to modern politics.
It uses the folktale form—particularly the elephant and tortoise narrative—as a structuring metaphor for political critique, demonstrating the continued relevance of oral tradition.
It uses folktales only for children's entertainment.
Folktales have no place in the play.
questions.explanation: The play's engagement with 'àló' (folktale) is central: the elephant and tortoise folktale provides the structuring metaphor for the entire political drama .

questions.text: What does the play reveal about the Yoruba concept of 'ìtàn' (history) and its relationship to political critique?
options: Ìtàn is irrelevant to the play's concerns.
The play operates as 'ìtàn'—a narrative that is both historically specific and allegorically universal—to critique power, demonstrating history's political utility.
Ìtàn is only about ancient events with no contemporary relevance.
Ìtàn has no political dimension.
questions.explanation: The play functions as 'ìtàn'—a narrative that is both historically grounded in Yoruba experience and allegorically universal—allowing its political critique to resonate across time and space .

questions.text: How does the play treat the Yoruba concept of 'orí' (destiny) in relation to Ajanaku's downfall, and what does this reveal about Yoruba cosmology?
options: Orí is fixed and Ajanaku could not have avoided his fate.
The play suggests that Ajanaku's character—his hubris and ambition—determines his fate, aligning with the Yoruba belief that character shapes destiny.
Orí is irrelevant to the play's concerns.
Only the gods determine orí and human action is meaningless.
questions.explanation: The play aligns with the Yoruba belief that character (ìwà) shapes destiny (orí): Ajanaku's arrogant character inevitably leads to his downfall, suggesting that he himself is the author of his fate .

questions.text: What does the play reveal about Yoruba attitudes toward leadership and legitimacy through its portrayal of Ajanaku's illegitimate succession?
options: Leadership is purely a matter of physical strength.
Legitimate leadership requires both traditional sanction (proper succession rites) and moral integrity, as demonstrated by Ajanaku's lack of both and the community's rejection of his rule.
Any strong person can be king regardless of legitimacy.
Legitimacy is irrelevant to leadership effectiveness.
questions.explanation: The play reflects Yoruba political philosophy: legitimate leadership requires proper succession (which Ajanaku lacks) and moral integrity (which he also lacks), making his rule fundamentally illegitimate .

questions.text: How does the play engage with the Yoruba concept of 'ìwà' (character) and its relationship to political legitimacy?
options: Ìwà is irrelevant to the play's political concerns.
The play demonstrates that ìwà (character) is the foundation of both personal and political legitimacy, and its absence leads to destruction, as Ajanaku's fate demonstrates.
Ìwà is only about outward appearance and has no moral dimension.
Ìwà has no connection to leadership.
questions.explanation: The play reflects the Yoruba belief that 'ìwà l'ẹwà' (character is beauty): Ajanaku's lack of good character undermines his political legitimacy and leads to his destruction .

questions.text: What does the play suggest about the role of women in traditional Yoruba political structures through characters like Iya Agba?
options: Women have no political role in Yoruba tradition.
Women like Iya Agba can wield significant moral and political authority, particularly as truth-tellers and leaders of resistance, revealing women's agency within traditional structures.
Women are always subordinate to men and have no influence.
Women only participate in domestic matters.
questions.explanation: The play presents a nuanced view: while patriarchal constraints limit women's formal political power, figures like Iya Agba demonstrate that women can wield significant moral authority and lead resistance movements .

questions.text: How does the play use the Yoruba concept of 'ẹbọ' (sacrifice) to critique political power through its portrayal of the Ijedodo ritual?
options: Ẹbọ is always portrayed positively as a sacred practice.
The play shows how ẹbọ can be corrupted from a sacred practice into a tool of political exploitation and violence, critiquing the perversion of tradition for power.
Ẹbọ has no place in the play.
Ẹbọ is only about animal sacrifice and has no political dimension.
questions.explanation: The play critiques the corruption of ẹbọ (sacrifice) from a sacred practice into the violent Ijedodo ritual, showing how traditional practices can be weaponized for political ends .

questions.text: What does the play reveal about the Yoruba concept of 'àṣẹ' (authority/power) through Ajanaku's illegitimate rule?
options: Àṣẹ is purely about physical force and has no moral dimension.
The play suggests that àṣẹ—the power to make things happen—must be legitimately acquired and morally exercised to be effective, as Ajanaku's downfall demonstrates.
Àṣẹ is irrelevant to politics.
Anyone can exercise àṣẹ without consequences.
questions.explanation: The play reflects Yoruba philosophy: àṣẹ (authority/power) must be legitimately acquired and morally exercised; Ajanaku's illegitimate and immoral exercise of power ultimately fails .

questions.text: How does the play engage with the Yoruba concept of 'ẹ̀rí' (evidence/truth) through Iya Agba's truth-telling?
options: Ẹ̀rí is irrelevant to the play's concerns.
Iya Agba's truth-telling and the eventual exposure of Ajanaku's illegitimacy demonstrate the power of ẹ̀rí (truth/evidence) to overcome tyranny's lies, affirming truth's political efficacy.
Ẹ̀rí is only about legal proceedings and has no broader significance.
Ẹ̀rí has no political dimension.
questions.explanation: The play demonstrates that truth (ẹ̀rí) is the ultimate weapon against tyranny: Iya Agba's persistent truth-telling and the eventual revelation of Ajanaku's illegitimacy lead to his downfall .

questions.text: What does the play suggest about the relationship between individual and communal responsibility through the community's eventual resistance?
options: Individuals bear no responsibility for communal outcomes.
The play suggests that tyranny thrives when individuals remain silent and that liberation requires collective moral action, emphasizing communal responsibility.
Only leaders are responsible for political outcomes.
Communal responsibility is irrelevant to the play's concerns.
questions.explanation: The play emphasizes collective responsibility: the community's silence enables Ajanaku's tyranny, and its eventual collective resistance brings him down .

questions.text: How does the play treat the theme of 'ìní' (possession/ownership) in relation to Ajanaku's seizure of disputed land?
options: Ownership is irrelevant to the play's concerns.
Ajanaku's seizure of disputed land reveals his greed and his confusion between royal stewardship and personal ownership, critiquing tyrannical appropriation.
The land dispute is a minor subplot with no thematic significance.
Only the king can own land legitimately.
questions.explanation: Ajanaku's decision to seize the disputed land for the royal house reveals his greed and his failure to understand that royal power entails stewardship, not personal ownership .

questions.text: What does the play reveal about the Yoruba concept of 'ìbá' (kinship/relationship) through Serubawon's relationship with Ajanaku?
options: Ìbá is always protective and beneficial.
The play shows how kinship ties—Serubawon's relationship to Ajanaku—can be perverted to serve tyranny, as Serubawon's parental relationship drives his corrupt kingmaking.
Ìbá is irrelevant to politics and has no role in the play.
Only biological kinship matters and has no social dimension.
questions.explanation: The play explores how kinship (ìbá) can be perverted: Serubawon's parental relationship to Ajanaku drives his corrupt kingmaking and ultimately leads to the destruction of his own family .

questions.text: How does the play use the concept of 'àdúrà' (prayer/invocation) in relation to political power, particularly through Ajanaku's invocation?
options: Àdúrà is always sincere and apolitical.
Ajanaku's use of invocation to demand the chiefs' support shows how prayer can be manipulated for political ends, critiquing the weaponization of spiritual language.
Àdúrà is irrelevant to the play's concerns.
Only priests can pray in the play's world.
questions.explanation: Ajanaku's use of Yoruba invocation ('If a cock crows on earth, its peers in heaven respond') to demand unconditional support reveals how traditional spiritual language can be weaponized for political manipulation .

questions.text: What does the play suggest about the relationship between tradition and change, particularly through its treatment of ritual corruption and authentic tradition?
options: Tradition is always good and change is always bad.
The play critiques the perversion of tradition while affirming the value of legitimate traditional governance, suggesting that authentic tradition provides resources for resisting tyranny.
Change is always beneficial and tradition is always oppressive.
Tradition is irrelevant to politics.
questions.explanation: The play distinguishes between corrupt manipulation of tradition (by Serubawon) and the legitimate traditional order that Iya Agba and Odejimi uphold, suggesting that authentic tradition provides moral resources for resisting tyranny .

questions.text: How does the play engage with the Yoruba concept of 'àkóbá' (taboo) through Ajanaku's violation of sacred limits?
options: Taboos are irrelevant to the play's concerns.
Ajanaku's violation of sacred taboos through the Ijedodo ritual demonstrates how tyranny breaks all moral and social boundaries, showing tyranny's fundamental lawlessness.
Taboos are only about food and have no political significance.
Taboos protect tyrants from criticism.
questions.explanation: The play shows how Ajanaku's tyranny involves the violation of sacred taboos (àkóbá), particularly through the Ijedodo ritual, demonstrating that tyranny recognizes no moral limits .

questions.text: What does the play reveal about the Yoruba concept of 'ìjìnlẹ̀' (depth/profundity) through Iya Agba's proverbial speech and the play's layered meanings?
options: Ìjìnlẹ̀ is irrelevant to the play's concerns.
Iya Agba's proverbial speech and the play's layered meanings demonstrate the Yoruba value of ìjìnlẹ̀—depth of wisdom and understanding—requiring deep engagement to fully appreciate.
Ìjìnlẹ̀ is only about physical depth and has no intellectual dimension.
Ìjìnlẹ̀ has no connection to language or wisdom.
questions.explanation: The play embodies the Yoruba value of ìjìnlẹ̀ (depth): Iya Agba's proverbial speech and the play's layered symbolism require deep engagement to fully appreciate .

questions.text: How does the play use the concept of 'àwòrán' (symbol/image) to convey its themes through powerful visual images?
options: Àwòrán is purely decorative with no thematic significance.
The play uses powerful images—the elephant, the generator shed, the fire—as symbols that convey its political and moral themes, demonstrating the power of visual symbolism.
Àwòrán has no meaning in the play.
Only visual art uses àwòrán.
questions.explanation: The play uses powerful symbolic images (àwòrán)—the elephant, the Ijedodo ritual, the fire—to convey its themes of tyranny, degradation, and destruction .

questions.text: What does the play suggest about the relationship between language and reality through Ajanaku's self-naming and Iya Agba's proverbs?
options: Language merely describes reality and has no creative power.
The play suggests that language—naming, proverbs, rhetoric—actively constructs political reality and can be used to legitimize or delegitimize power, demonstrating language's performative dimension.
Language is irrelevant to politics.
Reality is independent of language and cannot be shaped by it.
questions.explanation: The play shows that language constructs political reality: Ajanaku's self-naming as 'elephant' attempts to create a new reality, while Iya Agba's proverbs expose the truth behind this construction .

questions.text: What does the play ultimately suggest about the possibility of justice in a tyrannical system, and what role does collective moral courage play?
options: Justice is impossible under tyranny and can only come from external intervention.
Justice is possible but requires collective moral courage and the refusal to remain silent, as demonstrated by Iya Agba's leadership and the community's eventual uprising.
Justice is automatic and requires no human effort.
Justice is irrelevant to the play's concerns.
questions.explanation: The play's resolution—the downfall of Ajanaku and the restoration of order—suggests that justice is possible under tyranny, but only through collective moral courage and the refusal to remain silent .

questions.text: How does 'Once Upon an Elephant' compare with Wole Soyinka's 'Kongi's Harvest' in its treatment of tyranny, and what does this comparison reveal about the evolution of Nigerian political drama?
options: They are identical in every respect.

Both critique tyrannical leadership, but Ademilua-Afolayan uses Yoruba oral traditions and a female truth-teller (Iya Agba) as central to resistance, revealing the evolution toward more culturally grounded and gender-inclusive political drama.
They have no similarities and belong to completely different traditions.
Soyinka's play celebrates tyranny while Ademilua-Afolayan's critiques it.
questions.explanation: Both plays critique tyrannical leadership, but Ademilua-Afolayan's play is distinctive in its extensive use of Yoruba oral traditions and its central female truth-teller, revealing the evolution of Nigerian political drama toward more culturally grounded and gender-inclusive forms .

questions.text: What does a feminist reading of 'Once Upon an Elephant' reveal about the play's gender politics, particularly through the characters of Iya Agba, Desola, and Omoyeni?
options: The play is entirely patriarchal with no feminist dimensions.
The play critiques patriarchal violence (the Ijedodo ritual) while presenting women as agents of resistance (Iya Agba) and complicating simple victimhood (Omoyeni's secret agency).
The play celebrates male dominance and has no feminist critique.
Gender is irrelevant to the play's political concerns.
questions.explanation: A feminist reading reveals the play's nuanced gender politics: it critiques patriarchal violence while presenting women as complex agents of resistance and survival .

questions.text: How does a postcolonial reading of the play illuminate its political critique of contemporary African leadership failures?
options: Postcolonial theory is irrelevant to the play's pre-colonial setting.
The play allegorizes postcolonial African leadership failures, using the pre-colonial setting to critique contemporary dictatorship, corruption, and sit-tightism.
The play celebrates colonial rule and has no postcolonial dimensions.
The play has no political dimensions relevant to postcolonial theory.
questions.explanation: A postcolonial reading reveals how the play uses its pre-colonial setting to allegorically critique postcolonial African leadership failures, particularly the 'sit-tightism' and corruption that have plagued many nations since independence .

questions.text: How does the play engage with the concept of 'the subaltern' through Iya Agba's marginalization and her eventual centrality to the resistance?
options: The subaltern cannot speak in the play and remains voiceless.
Iya Agba, despite being dismissed as 'insane' and exiled, speaks truth to power and becomes central to the resistance, suggesting the play gives voice to the marginalized.
Only male characters speak in the play.
The subaltern is absent from the play.
questions.explanation: The play engages with subalternity through Iya Agba, whose truth-telling persists despite her marginalization, and who becomes central to the community's liberation .

questions.text: What does a psychoanalytic reading of Ajanaku reveal about his obsession with immortality and his violent sexuality?
options: Ajanaku is psychologically healthy with no deep-seated issues.

Ajanaku's obsession with immortality and his violent sexuality suggest deep-seated insecurity and a pathological need to prove his legitimacy, making his tyranny a compensation for perceived inadequacy.
Ajanaku is motivated purely by political ambition with no psychological depth.
Psychoanalysis is irrelevant to the play.
questions.explanation: A psychoanalytic reading suggests that Ajanaku's obsession with immortality and his violent sexuality stem from deep insecurity about his illegitimate origins, making his tyranny a pathological compensation for his perceived inadequacy .

questions.text: How does a Marxist reading of the play reveal its critique of political economy and class-based oppression?
options: Marxist theory is irrelevant to the play's concerns.
The play critiques the concentration of power and resources in the hands of a corrupt elite (Ajanaku, Serubawon) at the expense of the community, revealing class-based oppression.
The play celebrates capitalism and has no critique of economic exploitation.
Class conflict is absent from the play.
questions.explanation: A Marxist reading reveals how the play critiques the concentration of political and economic power in the hands of a corrupt elite, with Ajanaku's seizure of land and exploitation of the community representing class-based oppression .

questions.text: How does the play use the concept of 'hegemony' in its portrayal of Ajanaku's rule through both coercion and consent?
options: Hegemony is irrelevant to the play's political analysis.
Ajanaku maintains power through a combination of coercion (violence) and consent (manipulation of tradition and bribery of elders), illustrating Gramscian hegemony.
Ajanaku rules only through brute force with no element of consent.
Hegemony is purely economic and has no political dimension.
questions.explanation: The play illustrates Gramscian hegemony: Ajanaku maintains power through both coercion (the Oguno incident, the Ijedodo ritual) and consent (bribery of elders, manipulation of traditional legitimacy) .

questions.text: What does a deconstructive reading of the play reveal about its treatment of binary oppositions like legitimate/illegitimate and tradition/corruption?
options: The play has no binary oppositions.

The play deconstructs simple binaries—legitimate/illegitimate, tradition/corruption—by showing how they are mutually entangled, as Serubawon corrupts tradition while authentic tradition provides resistance.
Deconstruction is irrelevant to African drama.
The binaries in the play are stable and unambiguous.
questions.explanation: A deconstructive reading reveals how the play troubles simple binaries: Serubawon corrupts tradition, but authentic tradition provides resistance; Ajanaku's illegitimacy is both hidden and revealed .

questions.text: How does the play engage with the concept of female agency within patriarchal constraints, particularly through Omoyeni's secret resistance?
options: Female characters have no agency in the play.
Iya Agba exercises significant agency as a truth-teller and resistance leader, while Omoyeni's secret affair demonstrates female agency within constraints, complicating simple victimhood.
Only male characters have agency in the play.
Agency is irrelevant to the play's gender politics.
questions.explanation: The play presents female agency in complex forms: Iya Agba's moral and political leadership and Omoyeni's secret resistance both demonstrate women's capacity for action within patriarchal constraints .

questions.text: What does the play suggest about the relationship between violence and political power through Ajanaku's reliance on violence and ritual sacrifice?
options: Violence is always effective and sustainable.
The play shows that violence—Ajanaku's tyranny, the Ijedodo ritual—is ultimately self-destructive and unsustainable, critiquing violence as a foundation for political power.
Violence is necessary for good governance.
Violence has no consequences in the play.
questions.explanation: The play critiques violence as a foundation for political power: Ajanaku's reliance on violence and ritual sacrifice ultimately destroys him, suggesting that sustainable power requires legitimacy and justice .

questions.text: How does the play treat the concept of 'the common good' in relation to individual ambition, particularly through Ajanaku's reign?
options: Individual ambition always serves the common good.
The play contrasts Ajanaku's selfish ambition with the community's collective well-being, arguing that legitimate leadership serves the common good.
The common good is irrelevant to politics.
Only the elite matter politically.
questions.explanation: The play affirms the concept of the common good: Ajanaku's tyranny is portrayed as a betrayal of collective well-being, while the resistance aims to restore communal flourishing .

questions.text: What does a reader-response approach reveal about the play's potential for different interpretations by different audiences?
options: The play has only one correct interpretation determined by the author.

Different readers may identify with different characters and themes—some may focus on Ajanaku's tragedy, others on Iya Agba's heroism, others on Desola's victimization—each producing different interpretations.
Reader-response theory is irrelevant to the play.
The play's meaning is fixed and cannot vary between readers.
questions.explanation: The play's richness allows for multiple reader responses: audiences may focus on Ajanaku's tragic downfall, Iya Agba's heroic resistance, or Desola's victimization, each producing different interpretations .

questions.text: How does the play engage with the concept of 'intertextuality' through its references to Yoruba folktales, and what does this add to the play's meaning?
options: The play has no intertextual references.

The play's references to the elephant and tortoise folktale create intertextual connections that enrich its meaning for audiences familiar with Yoruba oral tradition, adding depth to its political allegory.
Intertextuality is irrelevant to African drama.
The play rejects all previous texts and traditions.
questions.explanation: The play's engagement with the elephant and tortoise folktale creates intertextual connections that reward audiences familiar with Yoruba oral tradition, adding depth to its political allegory .

questions.text: What does a structuralist reading of the play reveal about its narrative patterns and tragic structure?
options: The play has no structure and is formless.
The play follows a classic tragic structure: rise of the tyrant, abuses of power, climax of resistance, and resolution through downfall, revealing its engagement with tragic form.
Structuralism is irrelevant to drama.
The play is formless with no recognizable patterns.
questions.explanation: A structuralist reading reveals the play's classic tragic structure: Ajanaku's rise to illegitimate power, his escalating abuses, the climax of collective resistance, and his downfall—following the pattern of classical tragedy .

questions.text: How does the play compare with other African tragedies in its treatment of the tragic hero, particularly Ajanaku as an anti-hero?
options: Ajanaku is a conventional sympathetic tragic hero like Oedipus.

Ajanaku is an anti-hero or villain protagonist, unlike classic tragic heroes, making the play a distinctive African contribution to tragic drama focused on communal liberation rather than individual suffering.
The play has no tragic hero.
Ajanaku is identical to classical Greek tragic heroes.
questions.explanation: Ajanaku is an anti-hero rather than a conventional tragic hero: his downfall evokes justice rather than pity, making the play a distinctive African tragedy focused on the community's liberation .

questions.text: What does the play suggest about the relationship between theatre and social change, particularly through its engagement with political themes?
options: Theatre has no social function and is purely entertainment.
The play exemplifies engaged theatre, using drama to critique tyranny and inspire collective resistance, demonstrating theatre's capacity for social change.
Theatre should only entertain and avoid political themes.
Theatre is irrelevant to politics and social change.
questions.explanation: The play exemplifies engaged, political theatre: it uses dramatic form to critique tyranny, affirm collective values, and inspire audiences toward moral and political action .

questions.text: How does the play treat the concept of 'history' in relation to 'myth,' and what does this reveal about the play's allegorical dimensions?
options: History and myth are completely separate with no relationship.
The play blends history and myth, using the historical setting and mythical elements to create a narrative that is both specific and universal, enriching its allegorical texture.
Myth is irrelevant to the play's concerns.
History is irrelevant to the play's concerns.
questions.explanation: The play blends history and myth: the historical setting provides specificity, while the mythical elephant-tortoise narrative provides universal meaning, creating a rich allegorical texture .

questions.text: What does the play ultimately suggest about the relationship between literature and politics, and what is the playwright's political commitment?
options: Literature should avoid politics and focus on aesthetics.
Literature can be a powerful tool for political critique, using aesthetic and cultural resources to illuminate and challenge abuses of power, revealing the playwright's commitment to social justice.
Politics and literature are completely separate spheres.
Literature has no political function and should remain apolitical.
questions.explanation: The play demonstrates literature's political power: it uses Yoruba oral traditions, dramatic form, and cultural symbols to critique tyranny and affirm the possibility of collective resistance and justice .

questions.text: How does the play engage with the concept of 'catharsis' through its resolution, and what emotional and moral effects does it produce in the audience?
options: The play produces no emotional effects in the audience.
The play delivers moral and spiritual relief as justice is restored, the tyrant falls, and the wounded are healed, producing catharsis and reinforcing the audience's moral commitments.
The play ends in unresolved despair with no catharsis.
Catharsis is irrelevant to African drama.
questions.explanation: The climax provides powerful catharsis: the tyrant's defeat restores order, heals the innocent, and validates moral courage, producing emotional relief and reinforcing the audience's moral commitments .

questions.text: What is the ultimate literary achievement of Bosede Ademilua-Afolayan in 'Once Upon an Elephant,' and how does it contribute to Nigerian and African drama?
options: She wrote a simple folktale intended exclusively for primary school children with no literary sophistication.

She successfully fused indigenous oral performance traditions, Yoruba mythology, and biting political satire to create a masterpiece on the tragedy of tyranny, contributing a distinctive voice to Nigerian and African drama.
She translated classical Greek drama into modern English without African references.
She documented the colonial history of big-game hunting in West Africa.
questions.explanation: Ademilua-Afolayan's achievement lies in blending indigenous oral theatre, myth, and satire into a timeless critique of power, contributing a distinctive and powerful voice to Nigerian and African drama .

questions.text: Which of the following best describes the genre of 'Once Upon an Elephant' and its relationship to Yoruba oral tradition?
options: romantic comedy with no political dimensions.
political tragedy drawing on Yoruba oral tradition—proverbs, folktales, and ritual—to critique tyranny and affirm collective resistance.
historical documentary with no dramatic elements.
domestic drama focused on family relationships.
questions.explanation: The play is a political tragedy that extensively draws on Yoruba oral tradition—proverbs, folktales, and ritual—to critique tyranny and affirm the possibility of collective resistance .

questions.text: What is the significance of the play's title in relation to its themes, and how does it frame the audience's expectations?
options: It is a random title with no meaning.
It evokes the Yoruba folktale of the arrogant elephant, signaling the play's central metaphor about power and downfall, framing the audience's expectations for a moral allegory.
It refers to a zoo and has no deeper meaning.
It is a children's story title with no political significance.
questions.explanation: The title evokes the Yoruba folktale of the arrogant elephant, signaling the play's central metaphorical framework for critiquing tyrannical power and framing the audience's expectations for a moral allegory .

questions.text: Who is the protagonist of 'Once Upon an Elephant,' and how does this character function as the play's moral center?
options: Ajanaku, the tyrant king, is the protagonist.
Iya Agba, the truth-teller and resistance leader, functions as the moral protagonist—the truth-teller and resistance leader whose courage drives the play's resolution.
Serubawon, the kingmaker, is the protagonist.
Desola, the victim, is the protagonist.
questions.explanation: While Ajanaku is the central figure, Iya Agba functions as the moral protagonist—the truth-teller and resistance leader whose courage drives the play's resolution .

questions.text: What is the primary setting of 'Once Upon an Elephant,' and how does it function as a microcosm of political dynamics?
options: Modern Lagos with no traditional elements.
pre-colonial Yoruba kingdom, functioning as a microcosm of Nigerian and African political dynamics, though its themes resonate with contemporary realities.
Colonial Nigeria under British rule.
fictional European kingdom with no African elements.
questions.explanation: The play is set in a pre-colonial Yoruba kingdom, though its themes resonate with contemporary political realities, functioning as a microcosm of Nigerian and African political dynamics .

questions.text: Which Yoruba oral tradition element is most significantly used in the play to develop its political critique?
options: Written historical documents.
Proverbs, folktales, and rituals, which provide a culturally grounded framework for critiquing tyranny.
Only songs and dances.
Only religious prayers.
questions.explanation: The play draws extensively on proverbs, folktales, and rituals from Yoruba oral tradition, using them as a culturally grounded framework for critiquing tyranny .

questions.text: What is the function of the Ijedodo ritual in the play's plot and thematic development?
options: It is a minor ceremonial event with no plot significance.
It drives Ajanaku's quest for immortality and leads to Desola's victimization and Ajanaku's eventual downfall, serving as the play's central symbol of tyrannical abuse.
It is a comic interlude that provides relief from political tension.
It has no function in the plot or themes.
questions.explanation: The Ijedodo ritual is the plot's central mechanism: it drives Ajanaku's quest for immortality, causes Desola's victimization, and ultimately leads to Ajanaku's downfall .

questions.text: How does the play resolve the conflict between tyranny and resistance, and what does this resolution suggest about the play's moral vision?
options: Tyranny prevails and justice is impossible.
Ajanaku is killed through collective resistance, Serubawon commits suicide, and legitimate order is restored, suggesting that justice is possible through collective moral action.
The conflict is unresolved and the ending is ambiguous.
External forces intervene to restore order.
questions.explanation: The conflict is resolved through collective resistance: Ajanaku is killed during the Jobele ceremony, Serubawon commits suicide, and the community moves toward restoring legitimate order .

questions.text: What is the significance of Iya Agba's exile and return in the play's symbolic structure?
options: It has no significance and is a minor plot point.
It symbolizes the suppression and ultimate vindication of truth and legitimate authority, demonstrating that truth cannot be permanently silenced by tyranny.
It shows that Iya Agba is powerless against the palace.
It is a minor subplot with no thematic significance.
questions.explanation: Iya Agba's exile and return symbolize the suppression and ultimate vindication of truth: her banishment represents the silencing of dissent under tyranny, and her return represents truth's triumph .

questions.text: How does the play use the character of Desola to critique patriarchal power and the politics of the body?
options: Desola is a one-dimensional victim with no symbolic function.
Desola's victimization by the Ijedodo ritual exposes how patriarchal systems sacrifice female bodies for male political ambition, representing a powerful feminist critique.
Desola is complicit in her own oppression.
Desola has no symbolic function in the play.
questions.explanation: Desola's victimization by the Ijedodo ritual is the play's most powerful critique of patriarchal power, exposing how systems of male dominance sacrifice female bodies and autonomy .

questions.text: What does the play suggest about the relationship between individual courage and collective liberation through Iya Agba's leadership?
options: Individual courage is irrelevant to collective liberation.
Individual courage, like Iya Agba's truth-telling, is essential to inspiring collective resistance and achieving liberation, demonstrating the interplay between individual and collective action.
Only collective action matters and individual courage is irrelevant.
Courage is not a theme in the play.
questions.explanation: The play emphasizes the interplay between individual courage and collective liberation: Iya Agba's persistent truth-telling inspires and enables the community's collective resistance .

questions.text: Which character represents the corrupt manipulation of traditional religion for political ends, and what does this reveal about the play's critique of institutional corruption?
options: Iya Agba represents the corruption of tradition.
Serubawon represents the corruption of traditional religion and ritual for political ends, revealing how tyranny corrupts the very institutions that should check abuses of power.
Odejimi represents the corruption of tradition.
Desola represents the corruption of tradition.
questions.explanation: Serubawon represents the corruption of traditional religion and ritual for political ends, orchestrating the Ijedodo ritual to maintain Ajanaku's illegitimate power .

questions.text: What is the significance of Ajanaku's confession about sleeping with the sixth virgin, and what does it reveal about his character?
options: It proves his innocence and shows he was tricked.
It reveals his full awareness of and complicity in the ritual's sexual violence, underscoring his moral corruption and removing any ambiguity about his villainy.
It shows his remorse and desire for redemption.
It has no significance for his characterization.
questions.explanation: Ajanaku's confession reveals his conscious participation in the ritual's rape and sacrifice of virgins, underscoring his moral corruption and removing any ambiguity about his villainy .

questions.text: What does the play suggest about the relationship between power and legitimacy through Ajanaku's illegitimate rule?
options: Power equals legitimacy regardless of how it is acquired.
Legitimate power requires proper succession and moral integrity; power without these is illegitimate and unstable, as Ajanaku's downfall demonstrates.
Legitimacy is irrelevant to power and only force matters.
Only physical force determines legitimacy.
questions.explanation: The play argues that legitimate power requires both proper succession (which Ajanaku lacks) and moral integrity (which he also lacks), making his rule fundamentally unstable .

questions.text: How does the play use the motif of the elephant to develop its themes of power, arrogance, and downfall?
options: The elephant is a neutral symbol with no thematic significance.
The elephant represents arrogant, power-drunk tyranny that is ultimately brought down by cunning and collective resistance, paralleling the Yoruba folktale.
The elephant represents gentleness and wisdom.
The elephant has no symbolic meaning in the play.
questions.explanation: The elephant symbolizes Ajanaku's arrogant, power-drunk tyranny, which the play shows is ultimately vulnerable to the cunning and collective resistance of the community .

questions.text: What is the dramatic function of the Jobele ceremony in the play's structure?
options: It is a minor event with no dramatic significance.
It serves as the play's climax, where the tyrant's ambitions are thwarted and justice is achieved through collective resistance and the victim's agency.
It is a comic interlude with no political significance.
It has no dramatic function in the play's structure.
questions.explanation: The Jobele ceremony is the play's dramatic climax: Ajanaku's quest for immortality is reversed, Desola reclaims her life, and the tyrant is killed—the moment of poetic justice .

questions.text: How does the play treat the theme of suicide through Serubawon's death, and what does this reveal about the play's moral vision?
options: Suicide is celebrated as a noble act.
Serubawon's suicide represents the inevitable consequence of a life built on corruption and deceit, functioning as the playwright's verdict on those who trade integrity for power.
Suicide is irrelevant to the play's moral vision.
Suicide is portrayed as heroic and redemptive.
questions.explanation: Serubawon's suicide represents the inevitable consequence of a life built on corruption, deceit, and the pursuit of power at any cost—the playwright's verdict on such a life .

questions.text: What does the play suggest about the role of memory in resistance through Iya Agba's persistent remembrance of traditional legitimacy?
options: Memory is irrelevant to resistance and should be forgotten.
Iya Agba's memory of traditional legitimacy and her refusal to forget are essential to inspiring resistance, demonstrating memory's political power.
Forgetting is the best response to tyranny.
Memory is only individual and has no collective dimension.
questions.explanation: Iya Agba's persistent memory of traditional legitimacy and her refusal to forget the truth about Ajanaku's origins are essential to inspiring and sustaining resistance .

questions.text: How does the play use the concept of 'destiny' to explore Ajanaku's downfall, and what does this reveal about Yoruba cosmology?
options: Destiny is fixed and Ajanaku had no choice in his actions.
The play suggests that Ajanaku's character determines his fate, aligning with the Yoruba belief that character shapes destiny and that individuals are responsible for their choices.
Destiny is irrelevant to the play's concerns.
Only the gods determine destiny and human action is meaningless.
questions.explanation: The play aligns with the Yoruba belief that character (ìwà) shapes destiny (orí): Ajanaku's arrogant character inevitably leads to his downfall, suggesting that he is the author of his fate .

questions.text: What is the play's ultimate moral message about the fate of tyrants and the possibility of justice?
options: Tyranny is inevitable and justice is impossible.
Moral integrity, truth-telling, and collective resistance can overcome tyranny, while corruption and ambition lead to destruction, affirming the possibility of justice through human action.
Violence is always the answer to tyranny.
Power is everything and morality is irrelevant.
questions.explanation: The play's moral message is that moral integrity, truth-telling, and collective resistance can overcome tyranny, while corruption and unchecked ambition inevitably lead to destruction .

questions.text: Why is 'Once Upon an Elephant' considered an important contribution to Nigerian drama, particularly in the context of WAEC's recommended texts?
options: It is the longest Nigerian play ever written.

It combines Yoruba oral tradition with contemporary political critique, creating a distinctive form of engaged, culturally grounded theatre that speaks to both traditional values and modern political realities.
It is the first Nigerian play ever written.
It has no particular significance for Nigerian drama.
questions.explanation: The play is significant for its innovative combination of Yoruba oral tradition—proverbs, folktales, rituals—with contemporary political critique, creating a distinctive form of engaged, culturally grounded African theatre .

questions.text: Which of the following best articulates the play's treatment of the relationship between power and morality, and what does this reveal about the play's political philosophy?
options: Power and morality are completely separate domains.
Legitimate power requires moral grounding; Ajanaku's immorality is inseparable from his illegitimacy, revealing the play's belief that political authority must be ethically grounded.
Morality weakens political power and should be discarded.
Power excuses all moral failings.
questions.explanation: The play argues that legitimate political power requires moral grounding: Ajanaku's illegitimacy and immorality are inseparable, and his downfall results from both .

questions.text: What type of irony dominates the play's treatment of Ajanaku's quest for immortality, and what does this reveal about the play's moral vision?
options: Verbal irony only.
Tragic irony: the quest for immortality leads directly to death, revealing the play's moral vision that hubristic ambition is self-destructive.
Cosmic irony without human agency.
Comic irony that trivializes the quest.
questions.explanation: The play employs tragic irony: Ajanaku's quest for immortality, which requires the violation of sacred limits, leads directly and inevitably to his death .

questions.text: Who serves as the play's moral center, and how does this character embody the play's values?
options: Ajanaku, who embodies the play's critique of tyranny.
Serubawon, who embodies the play's critique of complicity.
Iya Agba, who embodies the play's values of truth, justice, and legitimate tradition against Ajanaku's tyranny.
Odejimi, who embodies the play's values of courage.
questions.explanation: Iya Agba serves as the play's moral center, articulating the values of truth, justice, and legitimate tradition against Ajanaku's tyranny .

questions.text: What does the Ijedodo ritual symbolize in the play's political critique, and how does it function as a symbol of tyrannical abuse?
options: The beauty of Yoruba tradition.
The corruption of sacred tradition for political ambition and the violent exploitation of women, making it the play's most powerful symbol of tyrannical abuse.
The power of the gods to punish sinners.
love charm with no political significance.
questions.explanation: The Ijedodo ritual symbolizes the corruption of sacred tradition for political ambition and the violent exploitation of women, making it the play's most powerful symbol of tyrannical abuse .

questions.text: What is the significance of the proverb 'The leper said two things of which one is a lie' in the play?
options: It warns against eating contaminated food.
Iya Agba uses it to expose Ajanaku's false claims and pretensions to legitimacy, challenging his self-presentation.
It is a prayer for healing.
It praises lepers for their wisdom.
questions.explanation: Iya Agba uses this proverb to expose Ajanaku's false claims and pretensions to legitimacy, challenging his self-presentation .

questions.text: How does the play treat the traditional African value of extended family solidarity, and what does this reveal about the play's social critique?
options: It glorifies extended family as flawlessly protective.
It critiques it, demonstrating how predatory relatives can exploit kinship for personal gain, revealing the play's critique of corruption within traditional structures.
It suggests extended family ties are nonexistent.
It claims uncles are always kinder than fathers.
questions.explanation: The play critiques the betrayal of kinship: Serubawon exploits his biological relationship to Ajanaku, and the community's ties to the palace are manipulated to enable tyranny .

questions.text: What does Iya Agba's role as truth-teller emphasize regarding personal ethics and the individual's responsibility to confront tyranny?
options: That people should abandon their communities.
That individual moral integrity and courage can transcend fear and challenge tyranny, emphasizing the moral imperative to speak truth to power.
That silence is golden and one should remain neutral.
That only the young can resist tyranny.
questions.explanation: Iya Agba teaches that even in the face of overwhelming tyranny, one must uphold moral courage and speak truth to power .

questions.text: What dramatic purpose does Bolaji's monologue in the generator shed serve? (Note: This question refers to the attached literature note, not 'Once Upon an Elephant')
options: It provides comic relief.
It functions as a classic tragic soliloquy expressing existential despair.
It reveals Makinde's bank account details.
It explains the chemical formula of narcotics.
questions.explanation: This question refers to the attached literature note ('The Drama of Taye & Bolaji'), not to 'Once Upon an Elephant'. The correct answer for 'Once Upon an Elephant' would be different.

questions.text: What literary device is present when Iya Agba's early warnings about Ajanaku's illegitimacy prove true?
options: Onomatopoeia.
Foreshadowing.
Metonymy.
Anachronism.
questions.explanation: Iya Agba's persistent truth-telling foreshadows the eventual exposure of Ajanaku's illegitimacy and his downfall .

questions.text: Which character represents genuine, disinterested moral authority in the play, and how does this character function as the play's ethical compass?
options: Ajanaku, who represents the consequences of illegitimacy.
Serubawon, who represents the consequences of complicity.
Iya Agba, who represents authentic moral authority, risking her safety to speak truth and protect the innocent.
Odegbami, who represents the hunters' guild.
questions.explanation: Iya Agba represents authentic moral authority, risking her safety to speak truth and protect the innocent .

questions.text: What constitutes the central dramatic climax of the play, and how does it represent the turning point in the struggle against tyranny?
options: The fistfight between Odekunle and Ajanaku.
The Jobele ceremony where Ajanaku's ambitions are thwarted and he is killed, representing the turning point where collective resistance defeats tyranny.
The love scene between Odekunle and Desola.
The initial ritual for Ajanaku's coronation.
questions.explanation: The Jobele ceremony is the dramatic climax: Ajanaku's quest for immortality is reversed, Desola reclaims her life, and the tyrant is killed .

questions.text: What does the symbol of the 'elephant' represent throughout the drama, and how does it function as the play's central metaphor?
options: Wisdom and patience.
Arrogant, power-drunk tyranny that is ultimately brought down by cunning and collective resistance, paralleling the Yoruba folktale.
Gentleness and kindness.
The beauty of nature.
questions.explanation: The elephant symbolizes Ajanaku's arrogant, power-drunk tyranny, which is ultimately destroyed by the cunning and collective action of the community .

questions.text: Why is the ending of the play characterized as tragic but morally satisfying, and what does this reveal about the play's ethical vision?
options: Because evil triumphs and injustice prevails.
Because the tyrant and his enabler are destroyed, restoring moral order, though at great cost, revealing the play's ethical vision that justice is possible through collective action.
Because everyone dies and there is no hope.
Because the ending is ambiguous and morally unclear.
questions.explanation: The ending is tragic in its cost but morally satisfying in that justice is served—Ajanaku dies and Serubawon commits suicide—revealing the play's ethical vision of justice through collective action .

questions.text: What social pathology is critiqued through the character of Serubawon, and how does this critique extend beyond the individual to institutional critique?
options: Urban traffic congestion.
The manipulation of religion and tradition for personal and political gain, critiquing how traditional institutions can be corrupted to serve tyranny.
Inadequate healthcare facilities.
High prices of petroleum products.
questions.explanation: Serubawon represents the corruption of religious and traditional authority for selfish political purposes, extending the critique to how traditional institutions can be weaponized for tyranny .

questions.text: How does the play depict the relationship between the individual and the community, particularly through the contrast between Ajanaku and Iya Agba?
options: The individual is always right and the community is always wrong.
The tyrant Ajanaku places himself above the community, while Iya Agba represents the community's collective wisdom and resistance, suggesting that true leadership serves the collective.
The community is irrelevant to political outcomes.
The individual should always submit to the community without question.
questions.explanation: The play contrasts Ajanaku's selfish individualism with Iya Agba's communal values, suggesting that true leadership serves the collective rather than the self .

questions.text: What moral contrast is established between Ajanaku and Odejimi, and what does this reveal about the play's ethical framework?
options: Both are tyrants and there is no moral contrast.
Ajanaku embodies tyranny and corruption, while Odejimi embodies principled governance and courageous opposition, revealing the play's ethical contrast between corruption and integrity.
Both are heroes and there is no moral contrast.
Odejimi is the villain and Ajanaku is the hero.
questions.explanation: The play contrasts Ajanaku's tyrannical rule with Odejimi's principled, courageous opposition, highlighting the moral difference between corruption and integrity .

questions.text: What is the thematic significance of Desola's rescue by Iya Agba, and how does it represent the triumph of wisdom over tyranny?
options: It shows that the gods are indifferent to human suffering.
It represents the triumph of wisdom and compassion over tyranny and violence, demonstrating that collective action and ancestral knowledge can overcome oppression.
It proves that Desola was never in danger.
It is a coincidence with no thematic significance.
questions.explanation: Desola's rescue by Iya Agba symbolizes the power of wisdom and compassion to overcome tyranny and protect the innocent .

questions.text: Which literary term best describes the staged rituals and public performances in the play, and how do they function dramatically?
options: Deceptive dialogue.
Spectacle and performance, functioning as sites of political struggle where power is both reinforced and contested.
Stream of consciousness.
Choric ode.
questions.explanation: The rituals and public performances are spectacles that serve both to reinforce power and to provide sites of resistance .

questions.text: What does the contrast between the legitimate Olubori rite and the corrupt Ijedodo ritual highlight about the play's distinction between authentic and perverted tradition?
options: All rituals are the same and there is no distinction.
The distinction between sacred tradition that upholds order and perverted ritual that serves tyranny, highlighting how tradition can be corrupted for political ends.
Rituals are meaningless performances with no moral content.
Only the king can perform rituals legitimately.
questions.explanation: The play distinguishes between legitimate tradition (Olubori) and its corruption (Ijedodo), highlighting how sacred practices can be perverted for political ends .

questions.text: What ultimate moral takeaway does the drama offer about tyranny, truth, and collective action, and how does this message remain relevant to contemporary Nigerian society?
options: That violence is the best solution to political problems.

That moral integrity, truth-telling, and collective resistance can overcome tyranny, while corruption and ambition lead to destruction, offering a message of hope and accountability relevant to contemporary governance.
That one should abandon family during hardship.
That superstitious beliefs are always accurate and should guide political action.
questions.explanation: The drama champions truth, moral courage, and collective action against tyranny, while exposing the self-destructive nature of corruption and unchecked ambition, offering a message of hope and accountability relevant to contemporary Nigerian society .
